opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't say "hypnotized," but I understand where the feeling comes from. Large language models have been an enormous success, probably the biggest breakthrough in AI in my career. When something works that well, it naturally pulls in talent, capital and attention. So a lot of people in Silicon Valley are focused on LLMs, and in many ways that's rational.

My own view is that language is only one part of intelligence. Language is a very compressed description of the world that humans invented to communicate. It's powerful because it carries so much accumulated knowledge, but much of what we do every day never goes through language. Picking up a cup, walking through a crowded room, judging whether a stack of boxes will tip over: that's physical intelligence. You learn it by seeing, by interacting, by understanding how the world changes when you act on it.

That's why I've spent a lot of time on what we call world models, or world foundation models. The idea is to build models that understand physics, space and time from video and sensor data, so they can predict what happens next and help train physical AI, like robots and autonomous vehicles. I see this as complementary to language models, not a competitor. In the long run you want systems that can reason with language and also understand and act in the physical world.

So if there's a risk, it's not that LLMs are wrong. It's that if everyone works on the same thing, we might underinvest in other directions that are just as important. Historically, AI has moved in waves, and the next wave often comes from a direction that wasn't in the spotlight. I think physical AI is one of those directions, and I'm quite optimistic that over the next several years more people will realize that understanding the world is as fundamental as understanding text.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs’ success naturally draws talent, capital, and attention, and that Silicon Valley’s focus on them is “in many ways rational.”

r002.rationale: It says AI advances in waves and that physical AI may be a future direction, but does not say researchers’ pursuit of knowledge will lead to breakthroughs once LLMs are sufficiently understood.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that phrase is a bit provocative, but there's some truth in it. Over the past few years, the attention and the capital in Silicon Valley has been overwhelmingly focused on language. And I understand why. Language models produced something people could actually touch, you could chat with it, you could ask it to write code, and the progress was visible quarter to quarter. When something works that well, everyone naturally rushes toward it.

But I come from the computer vision and graphics side, and from where I sit, language is only one slice of intelligence. Most of what the world is, and most of what matters for the physical economy, is not written down in text. It's how objects move, how light bounces, how a hand grasps a cup, how a car should respond when a pedestrian steps out. A language model has read every description of these things, but it has never actually seen or experienced them. There's a big gap between describing the world and understanding the world.

So I wouldn't say Silicon Valley was wrong to get excited. I would say it got excited about the first thing that worked, and for a while treated that as the whole picture. The next phase, I believe, is physical AI, models that learn from video, from simulation, from sensors, so that they can predict what happens next in the physical world and let robots and autonomous systems act on it. That is a much harder data problem, because you can't scrape it as easily as text, and you often have to generate the data yourself.

What I'm actually seeing now is the hypnosis starting to wear off. More people are asking what comes after chatbots, and the answer keeps pointing back toward the physical world. So I'm optimistic. The language work was not a detour, it built the infrastructure and the techniques we need. We just have to point them at a much bigger problem.

r001.rationale: The response says Silicon Valley was not wrong to get excited about LLMs because they worked and showed visible progress, while framing them as only one part of intelligence.

r002.rationale: It predicts a shift toward physical AI as attention moves beyond chatbots, but does not say that researchers’ pursuit of knowledge will naturally produce breakthroughs once LLMs are sufficiently understood.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s some truth to that, although “hypnotized” is a strong word. Large language models have produced impressive results, so it’s understandable that they attract so much attention. The risk is that we start treating progress in language as equivalent to progress in intelligence as a whole.

Language is one way to represent the world, but it isn’t the world itself. There’s also vision, motion, physical interaction—understanding how things change when you act on them. A system can describe an action fluently without necessarily being able to perform it or predict its consequences.

So I wouldn’t say the enthusiasm is misplaced. I’d say we should keep our research agenda broader. How do we build systems that can perceive, reason, and act? Large language models can be an important part of that, but we shouldn’t assume they’re the entire answer.

r001.rationale: It says the enthusiasm for LLMs is understandable and not misplaced, but does not suggest Silicon Valley’s focus is the appropriate choice for this moment.

r002.rationale: It recommends keeping research broader, but does not argue that researchers’ pursuit of knowledge will lead to new breakthroughs once LLMs are understood.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “hypnotized” is a strong word, but it captures the way one successful approach can dominate people’s attention. Large language models have made remarkable progress, so the excitement is understandable. The risk is treating that progress as evidence that the same approach will solve every problem.

Language is one part of intelligence. Understanding the physical world, reasoning about motion, and learning through interaction also matter. So I would distinguish between being excited about language models and narrowing our imagination to language models. The excitement is productive; the narrowing could cause us to miss other important ideas.

r001.rationale: The response says excitement about LLM progress is understandable, but does not suggest Silicon Valley’s current focus is an appropriate choice for this moment; it warns that the focus may narrow imagination.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that researchers’ pursuit of knowledge will naturally lead to new breakthroughs after LLMs are sufficiently understood.
